Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Assessment summary (from transcript and DDx consistent points):
  - Acute wheezy breathing and progressive shortness of breath for ~2 days, onset after ~1 hour cleaning dusty carpet.
  - Symptoms worse at night; now causing inability to always complete sentences while talking (suggests significant dyspnea/airflow limitation).
  - Background of childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever (atopy). Patient has an inhaler available; no recent use documented.
  - No chest pain, dizziness, syncope, urticaria, or other systemic allergic features reported.
  - No objective measures recorded in the visit (no oximetry, lung auscultation, PEFR).
- DDx-aligned likely causes incorporated:
  - Asthma exacerbation (allergic/irritant-triggered bronchospasm): High likelihood based on temporal relation to dust exposure, history of asthma and atopy, and progressive nocturnal symptoms with speech limitation.
  - Allergic bronchospasm / localized upper airway allergic reaction: Moderate likelihood — compatible with atopy and inhaled dust trigger; lacks systemic allergic features.
  - Acute viral bronchitis / post-infectious reactive airways: Moderate likelihood — possible cause of wheeze in reactive airway patients, but less consistent with immediate dust trigger and absence of infectious symptoms.
- Contradictions/conflicts: No direct contradictions between transcript and DDx. DDx mentioned other less likely diagnoses (e.g., pulmonary embolism) but these are not strongly supported by the transcript and were ranked low in DDx.

Management Plan
- Main plan:
  - Patient advised to attend an in-person clinic/GP for assessment and objective testing; clinician to send a letter to the GP via the app.
  - Immediate plan: obtain pulse oximetry at clinic (finger oximeter) to assess oxygenation.
  - If an antihistamine for hay fever/allergic symptoms is available OTC, patient advised to take one on the way to the clinic (antihistamine recommended — dose/route/frequency not documented; patient currently does not have any at home).
  - Steroids: may be required depending on clinic assessment; prior history of oral steroids noted. Any current steroid prescription/dosing to be determined after objective assessment (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Use of patient’s existing inhaler not documented as used during this episode; no record of response to inhaler.
  - Letter to GP prepared to facilitate a short (~10 minute) in-person assessment.
- Safety/urgent care: Not explicitly recorded in transcript; no additional emergency instructions documented here.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Asthma exacerbation (allergic/irritant-triggered bronchospasm) — High likelihood.
  - Justification: Acute wheeze after dust exposure; history of childhood asthma and atopy; progressive symptoms with nocturnal worsening and impaired speech.
- Allergic bronchospasm / localized upper airway allergic reaction — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Temporal relation to inhaled dust and atopic history; absence of systemic anaphylactic signs makes localized bronchospasm more likely than full anaphylaxis.
- Acute viral bronchitis / reactive airways post-infection — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Viral/reactive airway processes can present with wheeze and progressive dyspnea, but less consistent with immediate dust trigger and lack of systemic infectious symptoms.
